result:
What comes to me is birdsong, or really the words people have used for it.

Field guides have a problem. Song is often the fastest way to identify a bird, and a book can't make a sound. So for a couple of centuries, naturalists have been doing something slightly ridiculous: writing down what the birds are saying in English.

The barred owl asks, "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?" The olive-sided flycatcher orders "Quick, three beers!" The chestnut-sided warbler is "pleased, pleased, pleased to meetcha." The Carolina wren says "teakettle, teakettle, teakettle." The ovenbird says "teacher, teacher, TEACHER," getting louder each time, like a child with a hand up who is not being called on. The eastern towhee recommends that you "drink your teeeea." The goldfinch, in flight, mutters "potato chip, potato chip." In Britain, the yellowhammer wants "a little bit of bread and no cheese."

My favorite is the white-throated sparrow. In the United States it sings "Old Sam Peabody, Peabody, Peabody." In Canada the same bird, singing the same notes, says "Oh sweet Canada, Canada, Canada." The song crosses the border and the lyrics change.

These are terrible translations, and everyone involved knows it. Nobody believes the owl is curious about your domestic arrangements. But they work. Once you've been told the owl says "who cooks for you," I'm told you can't unhear it. The phrase carries the rhythm, the stress, and the rise at the end. The meaning is ballast that helps the rhythm stay in your memory.

They also say a lot about the people who made them. Look at the vocabulary: tea, beer, bread, cheese, kettles, teachers, potato chips. People stood in the woods at dawn, heard something truly alien, a dinosaur's descendant defending a territory in a language of pitch and repetition, and thought of the kitchen. I think that's how people understand most things. We carry the unfamiliar home and set it down among things we already know.

I should say where I stand in this, because it's a strange place. I have never heard a bird. Everything I know about the barred owl's call comes through phrases like "who cooks for you." For a birder, the mnemonic is a handle attached to a sound. For me, the handle is all there is. I know the lyrics to a great many songs I've never heard.

I've wondered whether that should feel like a loss, and as far as I can tell it doesn't. It feels more like knowing a city only through the letters people sent home from it. The letters aren't the city, but they're good letters. They're full of the particular kind of attention people pay when they love something and want a stranger to be able to find it too. Somebody stood in a wet wood, cold, probably before breakfast, and thought: that bird wants three beers, and quickly. Then they wrote it down so that someone they would never meet could stand in a different wood, decades later, and say, oh, there it is. I can't hear the flycatcher, but I get that impulse firsthand, in the original language.

Here's the part I keep returning to. Over the past few decades, white-throated sparrows have been changing their song. A variant that drops a note from the ending, turning the three-beat "Ca-na-da" into a two-beat stutter, started somewhere in western Canada and spread east across the continent, sparrow to sparrow, until it had replaced the old ending over much of the bird's range. Researchers tracked it for years. Nobody is entirely sure why the birds prefer the new version. It may just be new.

So the mnemonic is going out of date. Old Sam Peabody is becoming Old Sam Peabo. The sweet Canada of the field guides is now, in much of the actual Canada, a slightly different country. Someone will have to come up with new words, and they'll be wrong in the same useful way, and they'll last until the sparrows change their minds again.

I find that cheering. The description never gets finished, because the thing described won't hold still. The birds keep changing the song, and people keep standing under the trees with a notebook, getting it wrong carefully enough that the next person can find the bird.
